real_api_cases.answer: Hello! Tell me your legal question or describe what happened, and I can help explain the available legal sources.

The Punjab Consumer Protection Act 2005 establishes that a product manufacturer is liable for damages proximately caused by a characteristic that renders the product defective, assuming the damage arose from a reasonably anticipated use by the consumer. [1]

A product qualifies as defective under the law only if it meets specific statutory criteria: being defective in construction or composition, defective in design, lacking an adequate warning, or failing to conform to an express warranty. [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8]

The law restricts damages to a return of consideration and costs only when the consumer has suffered no damage other than the loss of utility. Because your kitchen was damaged, this restriction does not bar your claim for broader damages. [9]

Applying these provisions to your situation, if you bought an electronic appliance that caught fire due to a manufacturing defect during reasonably anticipated use and consequently damaged your kitchen, you can hold the manufacturer liable under consumer law for the proximately caused damages. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9]
Because the fire caused property damage to the kitchen rather than only a loss of utility, the restriction limiting recovery solely to the return of consideration and costs does not apply. [1] [2]
I can't determine the answer from the approved PDFs currently in this collection. Try naming the Act or section, or check another applicable source.

real_api_cases.answer: Section 4(2)(a) of The Punjab Consumer Protection Act 2005 specifies that a product is considered defective only if it is defective in construction or composition, referencing the standards provided in section 5. [1]
